title: Introduction to organic certification and internal control systems

lessons.title: What organic certification is and why it matters
lessons.html:
Organic farming in brief

Organic farming produces food without synthetic fertilisers, synthetic pesticides, genetically modified organisms (GMOs), and with strict limits on veterinary drug use and additives. It relies on soil building, crop rotation, composting, biological pest control and high animal welfare.

What certification means

Anyone can say their produce is organic. Certification is proof: an independent certification body inspects the farm against a written organic standard and, if the farm complies, issues a certificate. This allows the produce to be sold and labelled as certified organic, often at a premium price.

Standards

Which standard applies depends on the market. Export markets each have their own regulations (for example the European Union and the United States have their own organic rules). Locally, standards and participatory schemes are promoted by organisations in the organic sector. The certification body or buyer will tell the farm which standard it must meet.

Key requirements found in most standards

  • Conversion period: land must be managed organically for a set period before its produce can be sold as organic. The length is set by the standard.
  • Permitted inputs only: fertilisers, pest control products and cleaning products must be on the standard's approved list.
  • Separation: organic and non-organic products must never be mixed (parallel production needs strict controls).
  • Buffer zones: to prevent spray drift and contamination from neighbours.
  • Records: inputs, field activities, harvests, sales and stock.
  • Traceability: every batch can be traced back to the field it came from.
  • Annual inspection and possible unannounced visits.

Benefits and challenges

Benefits include premium prices, access to niche markets and improved soil health. Challenges include certification costs, yield dips during conversion, extra paperwork and pest control without synthetic chemicals.

lessons.title: Internal control systems (ICS)
lessons.html:
What is an ICS?

An internal control system is a documented quality system that a group of producers, or a large farm, uses to make sure every member or unit follows the organic standard. It is especially used for group certification of small-scale farmers, where inspecting every farmer externally would be too expensive. The certification body inspects the ICS and a sample of farms, and relies on the ICS to control the rest.

Parts of an ICS

  • Internal standards: the organic rules written in simple, local language.
  • Registration of members: each farmer signs an agreement to follow the rules.
  • Farm records: a farm map, field history, inputs used and harvest estimates.
  • Internal inspections: trained internal inspectors visit every farm at least once a year and complete a checklist.
  • Approval committee: reviews inspection reports and decides whether each farmer is approved.
  • Sanctions: clear consequences for breaking rules, from warnings to exclusion.
  • Training: for farmers, inspectors and staff.
  • Buying and handling controls: only approved farmers' produce is bought; quantities are checked against estimates; organic produce is kept separate and labelled.

Your role

At this level you may be a farmer member, a field officer or an internal inspector. You must:

  • Know and follow the internal standard.
  • Keep accurate records honestly.
  • Never bring prohibited inputs onto organic fields.
  • Report problems, such as spray drift from a neighbour, immediately.
  • Keep organic produce separate in harvesting, storage and transport.

One farmer breaking the rules can put the whole group's certificate at risk, which is why internal controls must be taken seriously.

Key points

  • Certification is independent proof that a farm meets an organic standard.
  • Standards require permitted inputs, separation, buffer zones, records and traceability.
  • An ICS lets groups of farmers be certified together.
  • Internal inspections, an approval committee and sanctions keep the group compliant.
  • One member's mistake can affect the whole group.
